chapter_title: Physical and Chemical Changes & Law of Conservation of Mass

m1_zero_omission_notes.chapter_executive_summary: Distinguishes physical vs chemical changes, verifies Lavoisier's Law of Conservation of Mass in closed systems through precipitation and gas evolution reactions.

detailed_section_hierarchy.full_explanation: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in any chemical reaction inside a closed system.

glossary_and_key_terms.definition: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

m3_practical_activities_lab_and_step_by_.activity_or_procedure_title: Verifying Law of Conservation of Mass using Barium Chloride & Sodium Sulfate
m3_practical_activities_lab_and_step_by_.objective_or_aim: Demonstrate total mass constancy during precipitation.
step_by_step_procedure: Hang ignition tube with BaCl2 inside flask containing Na2SO4.
Seal cork tightly and weigh initial mass M1.
Tilt flask to mix solutions forming white BaSO4 precipitate.
m3_practical_activities_lab_and_step_by_.expected_observations_or_working: White precipitate forms; scale reading M2 equals M1 perfectly.
m3_practical_activities_lab_and_step_by_.scientific_or_logical_conclusion: Chemical reactions undergo structural rearrangement without mass loss or creation.

scripted_dialogues.speech_text: When 5.3 g of sodium carbonate reacts with 6.0 g of ethanoic acid in a closed flask, what is the expected total mass of products?

scripted_dialogues.speaker: Student
scripted_dialogues.speech_text: Exactly 11.3 g! According to Lavoisier's Law of Conservation of Mass, the total mass of products must equal the total mass of reactants.

formula_calculator.formula: Mass of Reactants = Mass of Products
formula_calculator.example: 5.3 g Na2CO3 + 6.0 g CH3COOH = 2.2 g CO2 + 0.9 g H2O + 8.2 g CH3COONa = 11.3 g.
